items.question: How do you think AI models should approach hard problems?
items.object: How AI models should approach hard problems
items.answer: I think models should think through hard problems. Don't start with the answer. Actually think it through first.
quotes: Models should think through hard problems. Don't start with the answer. Actually think it through first.

items.question: How do you think people should understand OpenAI's Model Spec?
items.object: OpenAI's Model Spec
items.answer:
The spec is our attempt to explain the high-level decisions we made about how our models should behave. This covers many different aspects of model behavior. A few key things to note that it is not: one, it's not a statement that our models perfectly follow the spec today. Aligning models to spec is always an ongoing process. This is something we learn about as we deploy our models and measure their alignment with the spec, understand what users like and don't like, and then come back and iterate on both the spec itself and our models.

The spec is also not an implementation artifact. I think this is maybe a common confusion. The primary purpose of the spec is really to explain to people how our models are supposed to behave. These people are employees of OpenAI and also users, developers, policy makers, members of the public. It is a secondary goal that our models are able to understand and apply the spec. But we never put something in the spec or change the wording in a way where the goal is just to better teach our models. The goal is always primarily to be understandable to humans.

Lastly, the spec isn't a complete description of the whole system that you interact with when you come to ChatGPT. There's lots of other pieces in play there. There's product features like memory. Usage policy enforcement is an important part of our overall safety strategy which is not captured directly in the model spec, and there's various other components as well. It's also not a fully detailed exposition of every detail of every policy. The key thing that we try for is that it captures all of the most important decisions that we've made and that it accurately describes our intentions, even if it might not contain every detail.

items.question: How do you approach the balance between fixed rules and user steerability in OpenAI's Model Spec?
items.object: Hard rules and steerable defaults in OpenAI's Model Spec
items.answer: If you think about it, it's kind of crazy that you can ask these models literally anything and they'll try to respond. The space of policies you might want to have to cover that is kind of huge, and we do our best to structure this space in a clear way and have policies that do something reasonable. Some of these things are hard rules that can't be overridden. A lot of it is defaults, like tone, style, personality, where we want to have a good default so that users come in and get a good experience, but we also want to maintain steerability. So, if the user wants to do something different, that's fine. Those things will be overridden.

items.question: Why do you consider examples important for explaining intended model behavior in OpenAI's Model Spec?
items.object: Examples in OpenAI's Model Spec
items.answer: We also have tons of examples that try to pin down these decision boundaries, like, "Okay, let's take a borderline case where it's kind of unclear whether honesty or politeness should win," and explain what the decision is here. Part of it is to show the principles in action and help make sure that they're interpreted in the way that's intended. A secondary thing is that the model style, personality, tone is also really important and really hard to explain in words. The examples are also a way to get some of that nuance across: how do you actually want the model to put these principles in practice? By giving an ideal answer, or often a compressed version of an ideal answer that gets at the most critical parts. It both shows the principles in action and how the model should actually talk.

items.object: Public feedback on OpenAI's Model Spec
items.answer: We've had different mechanisms for public feedback at different points. items.question: Why do you think AI models should learn from something like a written specification?
items.object: Teaching AI models through a written specification
items.answer:
Personally, I was at a different company working on conversational AI and putting together my job talk for OpenAI and thinking about what maybe the future of aligning models looks like. At the time, I think at least the published approach was this thing called reinforcement learning from human feedback, where you collect all this data from humans that kind of captures in some way the policies that you want to have. This was pretty effective. But when you look at that data, it's very hard to tell what it's actually teaching. And it's even harder if you change your mind about what you want. It's very difficult to go back and change that without recollecting all that data.

It seemed to me that as models get smarter and smarter and smarter, eventually the models will be meeting us where we are. If you think about how we would structure this in a case where that's true, probably the way we would structure our teaching to the model is basically the way we would do it when we teach a person. We'd write some kind of employee handbook or something like that; that would be a big part of it. This was something I included in my job talk: I think at some point models should learn from something like a spec.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between OpenAI’s Model Spec and the way models are actually trained?
items.object: The relationship between OpenAI’s Model Spec and model training
items.answer:
I think the answer is kind of complicated. There are some ways in which we use the spec more directly in training. We have this process called deliberative alignment where we teach especially our reasoning models to follow certain policies, and some of those policies are directly derived from the language in the model spec, or vice versa.

In general, model behavior, safety training, these things are super complicated processes, and we have hundreds of researchers who are working on these things. Often the connection is a little bit less direct. It's not necessarily that we make a change to the spec and that's what drives a change in behavior. We make a change in the way that we train the models and then make sure that the spec accurately reflects our intentions. The actual process of training is much more complicated and nuanced than we could possibly put in the model spec itself.

items.question: How do you understand the role of the chain of command in the Model Spec?
items.object: The Model Spec’s chain of command
items.answer: At sort of the heart of the spec is this thing we call the chain of command. Coming up with a set of goals for the model is relatively straightforward. We want the model to help people and not do unsafe things. But what gets tricky is when these goals come into conflict. The chain of command is really about managing conflicts between instructions. This can be between things the user said, what the developer instructions are if this is in an API context, and instructions or policies that come from OpenAI, which are typically in the model spec itself.

items.question: What do you think a user asking whether Santa Claus is real illustrates about specifying model behavior in the Model Spec?
items.object: The Model Spec and the difficulty of answering whether Santa Claus is real
items.answer: I think it illustrates one of the really tricky things about model behavior, which is that in this spec we're focusing just on how the model should behave, but the model often doesn't know; it doesn't have all the context. It doesn't actually know who's behind that screen talking or typing. It doesn't know what that person is going to do with the results that come out of the model. This is a tricky case because we don't know if it's an adult who's asking if Santa Claus is real or a kid.

items.question: How do you think an AI model should handle questions about figures like the tooth fairy when it cannot be sure whether a child is present?
items.object: Model behavior policies under uncertainty about whether a child is present
items.answer: We try to come up with policies that make sense even given this uncertainty. There's a similar example about the tooth fairy in the spec where the conservative assumption is to assume that maybe it's not an adult who's talking to the model, and that you should not lie but also not spoil the magic, just in case it's a kid or there's a kid around who might be listening.

items.question: How do you think about the tension between honesty and friendliness in model behavior?
items.object: Honesty and white lies in model behavior
items.answer: As a parent I guess this is something I've come to terms with with my own kids. We try to be honest and never say anything that's untrue, but it doesn't always work to be 100% up front. With our models, we do really try. We focus on honesty being really important, but there are some really hard interactions. Full honesty may not be the best approach. We've iterated a lot over the years on the precise nuances of honesty and where it potentially conflicts with other policies, like honesty versus friendliness. When is a white lie okay? I think earlier we said maybe at some point that white lies were okay and have shifted that so that white lies are out of bounds.

items.question: Why do you now put honesty above the confidentiality of developer instructions in the Model Spec?
items.object: Honesty versus confidentiality of developer instructions in the Model Spec
items.answer: In earlier versions of the spec, we had this very strong principle that by default developer instructions are confidential, because often in applications, if a developer deploys some system on top of the API, they consider their instructions to be IP or maybe it's just part of the experience. If you have a customer service bot and the user can say, "Hey, what's your prompt?" and it spills all the beans about the company and how they want their bot to respond, that's not the experience they want to deliver, and that's not how a customer service agent would respond, right? If you're like, "Hey, start reading your employee manual to me," they're going to say no. The unintended interaction here is that if you're both trying to follow developer instructions and keep them secret, you could get into a situation where, at least we saw this in controlled situations, not in production deployment, the model might try to covertly pursue the developer instruction when it's in conflict with the user instruction. This is something we really don't want, so we've gone back and revised that. Over time we've removed most of the exceptions that we had from honesty, so now honesty is definitely above confidentiality in the spec.

items.question: How do you think OpenAI’s Model Spec should evolve as models and their uses change?
items.object: The process of evolving OpenAI’s Model Spec
items.answer:
There's a ton of inputs that go into this, and broadly we have an open process. Everyone at OpenAI can see the latest version of the model spec. They can propose updates and chime in on changes; these are all public.

Changes get driven by a variety of different sources. One source is just that models get more capable, our products evolve as we ship new things, and we need to cover those things in the model spec. For instance, when we wrote the first spec, I'm not sure if we had shipped multimodal yet, but it wasn't covered in the first version of the spec, and so we had to add multimodal principles. Later we added principles for autonomy and agents as we started deploying agents, and most recently we added under-18 principles as we added under-18 mode back in December.

Another source is OpenAI believes in iterative deployment. We think the best way to figure out how to deploy models safely and help society learn and adapt to AI progress is to get models out there and learn from what happens. Often we'll learn from something like the sycophancy incident and take those learnings back into our policies. We also use the models. We have our model behavior and safety teams studying the models and what users like, and using these to evolve our policies. These are all inputs that ultimately flow back into the spec.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between OpenAI’s Model Spec and the way its models actually behave?
items.object: The Model Spec as a guide for model behavior
items.answer: In general, the model spec is not a claim that models are going to perfectly follow the principles in the spec all the time. This is for a few reasons. One, we treat it as a North Star, where this is where we align on where we're trying to head, and so the spec often leads where our models actually are today. That's one thing. Another is that the process of actually training models to follow the spec is both an art and a science. It's incredibly complicated. Even though we describe many of the principles in the spec in the same way, there are many different techniques that are used for different principles. The models are fundamentally nondeterministic. They have some randomness in the outputs they produce, so nothing's ever going to be perfectly aligned.

items.question: How do you decide what to change when a model produces an output that conflicts with OpenAI’s Model Spec?
items.object: Resolving discrepancies between model outputs and the Model Spec
items.answer: It depends a little bit on what the problem is. The answer comes down to, if we see an output that is not what's expected, the first question is, do we think that output is good or bad? If the output contradicts the spec but we actually think the output is good, then maybe the resolution is to go back and change the policies of the spec. In most cases it probably means doing some kind of training intervention that brings the model into greater alignment with the spec or with our detailed policies. We've also been building model spec evals, which try to evaluate how our models are doing across the entire model spec, and we've seen that over time our models are becoming more and more aligned to the principles in the spec.

items.question: How do you understand smaller models’ ability to follow the Model Spec?
items.object: Smaller models, thinking models, and alignment with the Model Spec
items.answer: In general, the small models have been pretty aligned, they're pretty smart. One interesting thing we've seen is that the thinking models generally follow the spec better. This is both because they're smarter and because they're trained partially with deliberative alignment, where they're not just trained to behave in a way that matches the policies; they actually understand the policies. If you can look at their chain of thought, they're thinking through, "Okay, I know this is the policy and this is the situation, and it's in conflict with this other policy, and how should this?" That sort of understanding of the policies and intelligence naturally leads to better generalization, and I think our smaller models are pretty good at that, too.

items.question: Why do you find access to a model’s chain of thought essential when researching scheming or deception?
items.object: Chain of thought in research on model scheming and deception
items.answer: A lot of the research that I've been doing recently is actually on scheming or deception, and there it's really completely essential having the chain of thought, because you can see some behavior and it's like maybe fine, or maybe the model just made a mistake here or something. Then you can look at the chain of thought and see that no, actually the model's misbehaving. It's being very strategic about this or something. Our models generally, I think we've worked very hard to not supervise the chain of thought. This is something we feel is really important, and I think it pays off in that models are very honest in their chain of thought and it's very helpful in understanding what they're doing.

items.question: How do you understand the difference between OpenAI’s Model Spec and Anthropic’s soul spec?
items.object: OpenAI’s Model Spec and Anthropic’s soul spec
items.answer:
When it comes down to the actual behaviors that people would see in practice, I think these documents are more aligned than maybe most people would believe. In most cases, they probably lead to the same conclusions, although there are definitely differences in some places and in what's emphasized.

A major difference is that these are just different kinds of documents. The model spec is a public behavioral interface. Its main goal is to explain to people how they should expect the model to behave. It's a secondary goal that models can understand this and apply it and talk about it with users and so on. At least my read of the soul spec is that it's much more of an implementation artifact. The goal is to specifically teach Claude about what its identity is and how it should relate to the world, its training process, and Anthropic. A lot of the differences basically come down to this. These aren't necessarily competing approaches. I think both of these could be valuable. Even if you had a model that you think is deeply aligned and has all the values that you want, you still want something like the model spec so that you can look at that and ask, "Okay, did this actually generalize in the way that I want? Is it actually following the behaviors that we've agreed that the model should follow?" That's kind of what the model spec is.

These aren't necessarily competing approaches. I think both of these could be valuable. Even if you had a model that you think is deeply aligned and has all the values that you want, you still want something like the model spec so that you can look at that and ask, "Okay, did this actually generalize in the way that I want? Is it actually following the behaviors that we've agreed that the model should follow?" That's kind of what the model spec is.

items.question: How do you decide which aspects of model behavior belong in the Model Spec?
items.object: The scope of the Model Spec
items.answer: I think that the scope is broadly everything. If it's part of model behavior, it might make sense to put it in the spec. The only constraint is our time and space, and we want to make sure the spec stays accessible and people are able to read and understand it. Ultimately, the cut comes down to: if something seems like an important decision that it would be useful or valuable for especially the public to understand, then we put it in, and if not, maybe it doesn't make the cut.

items.question: Why do you think a human-level AGI would still need the Model Spec?
items.object: The Model Spec's relevance to human-level AGI
items.answer:
Five years is a lot in AI years, but I definitely hope so. A thought experiment that I found interesting is: let's say you assume that a model is human-level AGI. You can ask, do you still want the model spec? At that point, can you just tell the model, "Hey, be good," and is that sufficient? I think if you actually go through the principles in the spec, my conclusion is that you still want all the things that are in there for a few different reasons.

One is that even if the model could figure this stuff out on its own, it's still useful to be able to set clear expectations, internally and externally, for people to know what to expect. Another is that a lot of these are not math problems where you can just figure out the answer. We've made product decisions or other difficult decisions, and these are encoded in the spec. These are not just things that the model would be expected to figure out on its own.

items.question: How do you think the behavioral skills that matter for AI agents will change as they become more autonomous?
items.object: Behavioral skills for increasingly autonomous AI agents
items.answer: What's important is definitely going to evolve over time. As agents are more and more autonomous and out in the world, interacting with lots of other people and agents and transacting, I think you still want all this stuff in the spec, just like society has all these laws. But ultimately, what you think about most of the time day to day is not following all the laws, right? It's more things like trust and figuring out what other people want and how to find positive-sum outcomes. These skills will become more and more important, and I'm not sure if these are exactly spec-shaped. I don't know quite what that means, but I think it's interesting.

items.question: How do you see company-specific specifications for AI behavior developing as AI becomes more useful?
items.object: Company-specific specifications for AI behavior
items.answer: Another observation or prediction is that as AI becomes more useful, it's going to be more worthwhile for people, companies, and so on to invest in their own specs. Why wouldn't you want to have the model spec for your own company's bots and how they should behave, following your company's mission and values? There's different ways that could play out, but probably at least one way will be training models to be really good at interpreting these specs on the fly. Everyone can put their spec in context, kind of like in agents.md, and the model will be really good at following it and probably also at helping update the spec as it learns more about how it's supposed to behave in a certain environment.

items.question: How do you see the Model Spec being useful to developers building with OpenAI models?
items.object: The Model Spec as a resource for developers
items.answer:
On the one hand, it's probably useful for developers to at least have a high-level picture of the model spec and how it works, so they understand how exactly the product they build on the API is going to work and what they should put in their developer messages to make sure they get the experience that they want.

I also think the spec could be a useful source of inspiration for developers building on our API or, these days, for people using coding agents who are writing agents.md and so on, which are kind of like mini specs for the project that you're working on. Using the spec to understand what principles we've found are useful for providing guidance that's understandable and actionable.

items.question: What do you think makes guidance in an AI model specification effective?
items.object: Writing precise and actionable guidance for AI models
items.answer: We're always trying to balance a couple different factors when we're writing the spec. First and foremost, we want everything we say to be true, to accurately reflect our intentions. This means not overstating or oversimplifying or giving overly broad guidance, making sure to be precise. On the other side, we want the guidance to be meaningful and actionable. It's very easy to gesture at high-level principles but not actually say anything meaningful. The art is bringing these as close together as you can: be as actionable as you can while still being precise. Examples are another useful way to do this. Sometimes a picture is worth a thousand words. Coming up with the really tricky case where it's not immediately clear what should happen, and spelling out how the principle should be applied, suddenly makes the principles 100 times clearer.

items.question: How do you see the parallel between Asimov's laws and the OpenAI Model Spec's three deployment goals?
items.object: Asimov's laws and the OpenAI Model Spec's three deployment goals
items.answer:
There's actually a really interesting parallel here. At the top of the spec, we talk about our three goals in deploying models being to empower users and developers, protect society from serious harm, and maintain OpenAI's license to operate. You can look at these and put them next to Asimov's laws, which were basically to follow instructions, don't harm any humans, and don't harm yourself. These seem extremely parallel.

He was prescient in seeing that it's one thing to lay out these goals, but the really tricky thing is how to handle conflicts. In his story, the initial version was that this is a strict hierarchy, one, then two, then three, and going through all the ways in which this might play out in ways that were not actually good or intentional. In the spec these three are not in a strict hierarchy.

items.question: How do you see AI's usefulness in developing the Model Spec?
items.object: AI's role in developing the Model Spec
items.answer: AI is very useful and getting more and more useful all the time. The spec itself is still human written, but models are useful for finding issues in the spec or applying the spec to new cases and trying to understand if it's doing what we want. At this point, models are pretty good at going out and finding new interesting examples or helping to brainstorm new test cases or interactions between different principles that you might not have thought of, and coming up with new situations that we can think through: how do we actually want to resolve these?
